tip: 'Oud' takes no ending after 'is' or 'werd': 'werd honderd jaar oud'. Before most nouns it adds '-e': 'oude'.
Weather takes a dummy 'het', like English 'it': 'het is mooi weer' = it is nice weather.
'Zijn' + 'van plan' = to plan – literally 'to be of plan'.
'Op bezoek bij' – 'bij' means 'at someone's place': 'bij ons', 'bij de dokter'.
To agree is 'het eens zijn met'; the 'het' and 'met' are fixed: 'het eens met jouw voorstel'.
'Moeite' takes 'met' for what is hard: 'moeite met de Nederlandse uitspraak' = trouble with Dutch pronunciation.
After 'dat' the verb moves to the end of the clause: 'dat jullie er zijn'.
'Allergisch voor' – Dutch uses 'voor' (for) with 'allergisch', unlike English 'allergic to'.
'Gezellig' is a famously hard-to-translate Dutch word meaning cozy/fun/sociable.
Motion verbs like 'aankomen' take 'is' in the perfect tense, not 'heeft': 'is aangekomen'.
You can put the emphasised part first; the verb still comes second: 'een sterke koffie drink ik'.
'Zijn' + 'in de war' = to be confused – literally 'to be in the tangle'.
'Zeker' takes a fixed 'van', which sits just before 'dat': 'er zeker van dat dit lukt'.
'Hebben' + 'een hekel aan' = to hate – literally 'to have a dislike of'.
With a het-word and 'een', the adjective drops '-e': 'een levendig nachtleven', since it is 'het nachtleven'.
After 'zijn', the adjective takes no ending: 'zijn heerlijk', not 'heerlijke'.
'Over' plus a time span means 'from now': 'over een uur' = in an hour.
Present tense covers the near future: 'bespreekt het rapport morgen' = will discuss it tomorrow.
After an adjective, use 'te' plus the infinitive: 'moeilijk te verklaren' = hard to explain.
'Zal' (from 'zullen') makes the future and sounds a bit formal; casual speech often uses 'gaan' instead.
'Naar school' drops the article, like 'naar huis' and 'naar bed': no 'de' before 'school'.
Dutch writes numbers below a thousand as one word: 'honderdtwaalf'.
Dutch glues nouns into one word: 'winkel' plus 'centrum' makes 'winkelcentrum'.
After 'wil' plus a direction, Dutch often drops 'gaan': 'wil niet naar buiten' = wants to go outside.
In the perfect tense the past form ('ontmoet') goes to the end: 'hebben elkaar ontmoet'.
Most regular verbs build the past form with 'ge-' plus '-d' or '-t': 'serveren' becomes 'geserveerd'.
Mark a route with 'van' and 'naar': 'van Amsterdam naar Rotterdam' = from Amsterdam to Rotterdam.
To go on holiday is 'op vakantie gaan'; the 'op' is fixed: 'gaat op vakantie'.
An adverb keeps the bare adjective form with no ending: 'draait langzaam'.
Some plurals change the vowel: one 'schip', many 'schepen', short 'i' to long 'e'.
